notes.body:
<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Certification staff cannot update subcontract timelines themselves, causing duplicate work when Project Coordinators do not update them proactively

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** Project Coordinators are responsible for maintaining subcontract timelines in
the project-tracking tool (PSE), but do not always update them proactively for every project.
Certification staff have no edit rights on these timelines themselves.
**Trigger:** A subcontract timeline needs to change or be kept current for one of the
participant's projects.
**Impact:** The participant must manually email the Project Coordinator to prompt a timeline
update rather than making the change herself, which she describes as duplicate work
("Doppelarbeit").
**Workaround:** Sending a manual reminder email to the Project Coordinator responsible for the
project.
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant describes this as a
recurring, unprompted current practice and explicitly names it as duplicate work.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 2
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P03

**Representative Quotes:**
> "Ja, also generell würde ich Rolle von der oder dem PC zu definieren, dass die wirklich in PSE die ganzen Timelines pflegen dafür zuständig sind ... aber jetzt für die Projekte von meinen Kunden, da also im Endeffekt, wenn ich hier nicht da regelmäßig schreibe ... passiert da nichts." - [P03]
>
> Translation: "Well, generally I would define the PC's [Project Coordinator's] role as being responsible for maintaining all the timelines in PSE ... but for my customers' projects, if I don't write there regularly, nothing happens." - [P03]

> "Das ist so, wo ich denke, das ist so ein bisschen Doppelarbeit ... wenn ich die Rechte hätte, in der Zeit, wo ich ihr dann noch mal die E-Mail schreibe, dass ihr die Timeline anfasst ... könnt ihr es einfach direkt selber updaten. ... Also entweder die machen es selbstständig oder uns werden die Rechte gegeben, da auch was anzupassen." - [P03]
>
> Translation: "That's where I think it's a bit of duplicate work ... if I had the rights, in the time it takes me to write an email asking them to touch the timeline ... you could just update it directly yourselves. ... So either they do it on their own, or we get the rights to adjust it too." - [P03]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- Granting certification staff edit rights on subcontract timelines, or ensuring Project
  Coordinators update them proactively without needing a manual prompt (P03). Explicitly
  unvalidated.

**Validation question:** Do other Auditors or Customer Specialists also lack edit rights on
subcontract timelines and need to manually prompt Project Coordinators to keep them current?

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** For customers with large Appendix ABC documents (e.g. 1,000-1,500 device
entries), the specific information actually needed to build the assessment plan and interact
with the customer is a small subset (requested certification, sites involved, product/
technology codes per site, sterilization/packaging/reprocessing details) buried within a much
larger volume of information that is not always necessary for planning. This is distinct from
Appendix ABC being incomplete or error-prone: the document can be fully and correctly filled
out and still require significant manual effort to locate the operationally relevant fields
within it.
**Trigger:** A Customer Specialist begins building an assessment plan or interacting with a
large customer's Appendix ABC.
**Impact:** Certification staff report reaching the practical limits of Excel when extracting
the needed subset from a large document, describing the excess information as "noise" that
must be manually filtered before the relevant "signal" becomes usable as an operational
interface.
**Workaround:** The participant maintains a personally built spreadsheet containing only the
essential fields, manually extracted from each customer's full Appendix ABC (see the related
positive-pattern research gap logged in [[../01_interviews/P06]]).
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant describes this as the
"real challenge" distinct from missing data, directly and in detail, across several parts of
the interview.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 3
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P06

**Representative Quotes:**
> "For me, the problem is not that there are some missing data. ... the real challenge ... is that the information we really need are somehow hidden within a large amount of information that are not always necessary ... this creates noise. ... there is a very small subset of information that we really need to create the plan and to be able to really interact with the customer." - [P06]

> "Typically, I manage customers that have an appendix ABC ... with at least 1000, 1500 or something like that [device entries]. ... It's not easy to manage that with a large Excel file, probably the Excel is not the right tool. ... We just need, for example, the requested certification ... which are the sites involved ... the relevant product and technology codes applied to each site ... and then some few more key details about the sterilization, packaging, reprocessing." - [P06]

> "I have a love and hate relationship with Excel in general. ... you really reach the ceiling very fast when you have to manage a large amount of data ... it's not probably the right tool with this back and forth to the customer." - [P06]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- Automatically extracting and surfacing only the small, essential planning-relevant data
  subset from the full Appendix ABC as the default operational interface (P06), converging
  with the broader Appendix ABC digitization vision logged under
  [[../03_pains/Appendix ABC is treated as single source of truth despite being the most error-prone document]].
  Explicitly unvalidated.

**Validation question:** Do other Customer Specialists/auditors also describe the essential
planning data as a small subset buried within a much larger volume of Appendix ABC
information, distinct from the document being error-prone or incomplete?

## Reference

<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Certification staff must manually verify auditor and assessor conflict of interest with no automated check

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** Certification staff must manually check whether an auditor or assessor has a
conflict of interest with a given customer (for example, through a subcontractor
relationship), with no tool support to flag or verify this automatically.
**Trigger:** The interviewer asks what other activities could be supported by the new software
beyond what has already been discussed.
**Impact:** The conflict-of-interest and independence check for the audit team is delegated to
the Customer Specialist, who must manually verify, for each relevant customer, whether the
responsible auditor/assessor has any disqualifying relationship (e.g. with a subcontractor).
**Workaround:** Manual verification by the Customer Specialist, checked against her own
knowledge of the audit team's relationships, with no automated cross-check.
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant describes a specific,
concrete, recurring compliance responsibility with a clearly stated absence of tool support.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 2
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P04

**Representative Quotes:**
> "One thing that I can probably, I don't know, because about, let's say, a conflict of interest and independence. Now we need to check by our own for the audit team. I mean, let's say in a relationship with subcontractor, I think that is delegated now to the customer specialist to check if the relevant responsible don't have responsibilities." - [P04]

> "This would be very useful to, let's say, avoid manual verification by the customer specialist to look if the assessor or the audit team don't have any conflict with the company." - [P04]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- An automated conflict-of-interest check that cross-references assigned auditors/assessors
  against known subcontractor and other disqualifying relationships per customer (P04).
  Explicitly unvalidated.

**Validation question:** Do other Customer Specialists also manually verify auditor/assessor
conflict-of-interest status (e.g. subcontractor relationships) against each customer, and how
often does this manual check need repeating (e.g. annually) per customer?

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Communication is not linked to a project object, requiring staff to manually reference project numbers

**Update (2026-08-13):** P07 directly confirms the same mechanism from a Project Coordinator
(commercial/backoffice) segment, but on the incoming rather than outgoing side: when a
customer request arrives without her copied, or before the corresponding project exists in
PSE, the related e-mails or documents "float around" and can no longer be properly assigned,
given the sheer project volume. Per [[Definitions]] "Theme threshold," this note is promoted
to theme
[[../02_themes/Communication is not linked to a project object, requiring staff to manually reference project numbers]]
with Confidence Basis Single-interview strong evidence → Multi-interview (2 of 7 interviews
processed so far; Confidence remains Medium since repetition is below the typical 3+ needed
for High). With 2 interviews and Severity Medium, neither condition in [[Definitions]]
"Severity/Confidence flag" applies, so `validation_status` and `validation_question` are
removed from the frontmatter.

**Theme:** [[../02_themes/Communication is not linked to a project object, requiring staff to manually reference project numbers]]
**Description:** Email and chat (Teams) communication about a project is not linked to any
project object. To make clear which project a message concerns, P02 must manually include a
reference, such as an SAP number or PSE project number, in every message. P07 confirms the
same missing link from the receiving side: if a request arrives without her copied, or if the
project does not yet exist in PSE, the associated e-mails or documents have no project object
to attach to and become effectively unassignable.
**Trigger:** P02 writes an e-mail or Teams message about a specific project. P07 receives a
customer request or related document either without being copied, or before the project has
been created in PSE.
**Impact:** P02: every project-related message requires manually adding a reference number,
adding small recurring friction to routine communication. P07: unassignable e-mails/documents
"float around" and, given the high volume of concurrent projects, can be difficult to reconcile
later.
**Workaround:** P02 manually includes the project/SAP/PSE reference number in each message. P07
tries to ensure she is copied on all project-related e-mail communication, since she is also
responsible for report dispatch and billing and only learns a report has been sent, or a
project can be (partially) invoiced, from that communication.
**Confidence Basis:** Multi-interview — two distinct interviews (P02, P07) from different roles
directly evidence the same mechanism: communication is not linked to a project object.

**Severity/Confidence flag:** Not applicable. Severity Medium with Confidence Medium does not
meet either condition in [[Definitions]] "Severity/Confidence flag"; no `validation_status` is
set.

**Related Evidence (2026-08-14):** P03 separately describes difficulty tracking which channel
(email or UCI, an internal customer/communication portal) was used for a given project
update, requiring her to note the channel manually in her own tracking list. This is an
adjacent but distinct mechanism (channel fragmentation vs. missing reference-number linking).
P08 directly confirms the same channel-fragmentation mechanism from a second interview
(escalation communication split across email, Teams, and UCI/PSE, described as "catastrophic"
to reassemble after time away), so this observation is now promoted into its own theme and
pain point:
[[../02_themes/Communication scattered across multiple parallel channels makes project history hard to reconstruct]] /
[[../03_pains/Communication scattered across multiple parallel channels makes project history hard to reconstruct]].
It remains logged here as related evidence only and does not increase this pain point's
interview count or confidence.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 2
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P02, P07

**Representative Quotes:**
> "Momentan muss ich es, also wenn ich eine E-Mail schreibe, Team [Teams] muss man sich immer die Projektnummer, irgendeine Referenz S.A.P. Nummer oder P.S.E. Projektnummer reinschreiben, dass ich 'ne Referenz irgendeinen Anhaltspunkt habe, welches Projekt geht es quasi." - [P02]
>
> Translation: "Currently I have to — so when I write an email, [or] Teams, you always have to write in the project number, some reference SAP number or PSE project number, so that I have a reference, some point of reference, [to know] which project it concerns." - [P02]

> "Ist es nicht der Fall, existiert dieses Projekt nicht im PSE, dann dümpeln die Dokumente irgendwo rum oder die E-Mails und können dann nicht mehr entsprechend zugeordnet werden." - [P07]
>
> Translation: "If that is not the case, if this project does not exist in PSE, then the documents or the e-mails float around somewhere and can no longer be properly assigned." - [P07]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
[None currently logged.]

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

notes.body:
<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Communication scattered across multiple parallel channels makes project history hard to reconstruct

**Theme:** [[../02_themes/Communication scattered across multiple parallel channels makes project history hard to reconstruct]]
**Description:** Project-related communication runs across multiple parallel channels with no
single linked record. P03 must manually track whether a given update was communicated by
email or through UCI (an internal customer-communication portal). P08 describes the same
mechanism across three channels — email, Teams, and UCI/PSE (an internal customer/project
tool) — and reports that reassembling this history after time away (e.g. a two-week vacation)
is very difficult. This is distinct from
[[../03_pains/Communication is not linked to a project object, requiring staff to manually reference project numbers]]
(P02, P07), which concerns communication missing a project-object/reference-number anchor
rather than fragmentation across channels.
**Trigger:** A project update or escalation is communicated through whichever channel is
convenient at the time (email, Teams call, or the UCI/PSE customer-communication path), rather
than a single consistent channel.
**Impact:** P03 must manually note which channel was used for each update in her own tracking
list, to avoid losing track of communications not confirmed by email. P08 describes
reassembling scattered communication after returning from time away as "catastrophic," and
separately reports that an internal escalation process spanning multiple communication paths
is itself communication-intensive, adding effort beyond the substantive decision it requires.
**Workaround:** P03 manually records the channel used in a personal tracking list. P08 has no
described workaround beyond manually retracing each channel.
**Confidence Basis:** Multi-interview — two distinct interviews (P03, P08) directly evidence
the same mechanism: project communication scattered across multiple parallel, unlinked
channels.

**Severity/Confidence flag:** Not applicable. Severity Medium with Confidence Medium does not
meet either condition in [[Definitions]] "Severity/Confidence flag"; no `validation_status` is
set.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 3
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P03, P08

**Representative Quotes:**
> "Meistens schreibe ich mir da irgendwie noch dazu, irgendwie via Mail oder via UCI, weil das ist jetzt auch immer, dann denkt man, hey, ich bin gar keine Mail dazu. ... diese zwei Kanäle sind auch manchmal eher ein Hindernis, dass man das irgendwie nachverfolgen kann." - [P03]
>
> Translation: "Usually I also note down whether it was via email or via UCI, because otherwise you think, hey, I don't have an email about that. ... these two channels are also sometimes more of an obstacle to being able to track it." - [P03]

> "Es gibt E-Mail-Kommunikationspfad, es gibt einen Teams-Kommunikationspfad, es gibt gegebenenfalls noch zusätzlichen Pfad über UCI beziehungsweise PSE[M] und Kunden. Diese Informationen nach zwei Wochen Urlaub wieder zusammenzusuchen, katastrophal." - [P08]
>
> Translation: "There's an email communication path, there's a Teams communication path, there is possibly an additional path via UCI or PSE and customers. Reassembling this information after two weeks of vacation — catastrophic." - [P08]

> "Dann muss ich über unseren Eskalationsprozess, ich darf jetzt offiziell nicht mehr an unsere höchsten Instanzen rangehen, dann muss ich da eine Person dazwischen nehmen, die muss entscheiden, ob ich es überhaupt weitergeben kann oder ob sie es selber klären. Das ist kommunikationsintensiv." - [P08]
>
> Translation: "Then I have to go through our escalation process — I'm officially no longer allowed to approach our highest authorities directly, so I have to bring in a person in between, who has to decide whether I can even pass it on or whether they'll clarify it themselves. That is communication-intensive." - [P08]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- A single tool with an in-tool chat/communication feature tied to the project object, so
  history does not need to be reassembled from separate email, Teams, and portal channels
  (P08, converging with a broader single-tool-overview vision). Explicitly unvalidated.
- A single-click forwarding/escalation action within the tool, replacing ad hoc phone calls and
  the multi-channel escalation process (P08). Explicitly unvalidated.

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Customer accounts are assigned informally without domain-fit criteria following staff attrition

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** While managers generally hold defined areas of responsibility, individual
customer accounts are currently distributed without significant, defined criteria: after a
wave of staff attrition (35 people left the organization the previous year), remaining staff
took on customers largely on a first-available basis, regardless of domain fit, simply because
there was more work than capacity.
**Trigger:** A customer needs to be assigned to a staff member, especially in the aftermath of
high staff attrition when many accounts become unowned at once.
**Impact:** Customer-account assignment is not based on domain expertise or fit, which the
participant implies as a quality/consistency risk, though no specific downstream error is
cited.
**Workaround:** None described; whoever currently has capacity takes on the customer.
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant gives a specific,
concrete example (35 departures in the previous year) and describes the current state as a
direct, unprompted observation.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 1
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P07

**Representative Quotes:**
> "Also die Führungskräfte haben in der Regel schon bestimmte Bereiche ... Aber die Kundenverteilung, wie sie im Moment stattfindet. Letztes Jahr sind ja 35 Leute von uns gegangen und jeder, der konnte, hat Kunden genommen, ja, egal in welchem Bereich, weil einfach so viel los war. Derzeit gibt es keine signifikanten Merkmale, wie Kunden verteilt werden, sondern derjenige, der die Zeit hat, macht das." - [P07]
>
> Translation: "Managers generally already have certain areas ... But how customer distribution currently happens: last year 35 people left us, and everyone who could took on customers, regardless of area, because there was simply so much going on. Currently there are no significant criteria for how customers are distributed; whoever has the time does it." - [P07]

notes.body:
<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Customer-facing Appendix ABC version conflicts arise from unshared local copies

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** Certification staff and customers each maintain their own local copy of
Appendix ABC; staff copies are stored locally rather than in a shared cloud location. Edits
made by one party (staff correcting the document directly, or the customer sending an update)
are not automatically visible to the other, producing version conflicts and a false sense of
alignment. This is related to, but a distinct mechanism from, two existing findings: staff
retrieval friction among colleagues in
[[../03_pains/No shared access to the current Appendix ABC version forces staff to rely on colleagues]]
(P02), and auditor-vs-Technical-Documentation-reviewer divergence at the submission step in
[[../03_pains/Independently-edited Appendix ABC copies between auditors and reviewers diverge, causing rejected certification submissions]]
(P05). This finding concerns ongoing staff-to-customer collaboration rather than
staff-internal retrieval or a specific submission step.
**Trigger:** A Customer Specialist or the customer edits their respective local copy of
Appendix ABC without the other party being aware of the change.
**Impact:** The participant reports receiving customer versions after having already made
direct corrections to their own copy, requiring reconciliation; describes feeling ownership
over "my" copy since it is not shared with the customer; and reports sometimes believing both
parties are aligned when they are not, because the document is not shared.
**Workaround:** The participant sometimes edits the document directly when confident in the
correct answer, then sends the update back to the customer labeled as "the last update," but
still sometimes receives modifications made against the older, previous version.
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant describes this
directly and repeatedly when asked about receiving conflicting Appendix ABC versions.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 2
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P06

**Representative Quotes:**
> "You mean I receive a version [conflict]? Yes, it happened quite a lot. Sometimes I also receive this document. I think it's mine somehow, so I fix some points. ... I hope to receive the modification that they did from the last I sent them. Yes, this is a problem." - [P06]

> "Yes, because it's a document inside my computer and I feel it's like one of the other Excels I have because Excel is not shared with them. It's not in a cloud, so I can only use them. ... sometimes maybe you are working and you think we are aligned, but we are not because it's not shared." - [P06]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- A single, jointly-editable device-list document shared between staff and the customer,
  eliminating separate local copies (P06), converging with the broader Appendix ABC
  digitization vision logged under
  [[../03_pains/Appendix ABC is treated as single source of truth despite being the most error-prone document]].
  Explicitly unvalidated.

**Validation question:** Do other Customer Specialists also report version conflicts with
customers specifically because their working copy of Appendix ABC is a local, unshared file
rather than a live shared document?

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

notes.body:
<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Customers apply their own definition of critical supplier, causing omissions or over-inclusion on Appendix ABC

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** The certification body uses an internal definition of "critical supplier"
that does not necessarily match the definition a customer applies when filling out the
critical-supplier tab of Appendix ABC. This is a definitional mismatch about which suppliers
qualify, distinct from the separately logged data-redundancy issue where the same
supplier-relevance data is duplicated and contradictory across sheets within one document (see
[[Appendix ABC internal redundancy across sheets produces contradictory supplier information]],
P02).
**Trigger:** The auditor reviews the customer's Appendix ABC critical-supplier list against
what is actually observed during the audit.
**Impact:** The mismatch is often only discovered at the audit itself, by which point a
company that should have been listed as a critical supplier was left off, or companies the
certification body does not consider critical were included instead. Either direction can
require rework of the supplier list after the audit has already started.
**Workaround:** None described beyond catching and correcting the mismatch during the audit.
The participant suggests showing the certification body's definition directly on the same
screen/tab where the customer enters critical suppliers, rather than on a separate reference
tab, as a possible mitigation.
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant describes both the
mechanism and its bidirectional impact (omission and over-inclusion) directly and specifically.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 1
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P05

**Representative Quotes:**
> "There's a tab in the appendix ABC for critical suppliers ... a lot of the time we'll discover at the audit that there's a company that they left off their appendix ABC that should be considered a critical supplier ... There's a definition of critical supplier that we use internally that does not necessarily match what the client may define for themselves as critical supplier. ... sometimes there's a mismatch between what they put on the appendix ABC and what we need to see ... that can go both ways, where they've left off companies that should be there and they've put too many companies on there that we don't care about." - [P05]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- Displaying the certification body's internal definition of "critical supplier" directly on
  the same screen where the customer enters suppliers, instead of on a separate reference tab
  (P05). Explicitly unvalidated.

**Validation question:** Do other auditors or reviewers also find that customers apply a
different definition of "critical supplier" than the certification body's internal
definition, causing suppliers to be missing from or over-included on Appendix ABC?

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

notes.body:
<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Customers cannot reliably predict the duration of the final certification review step

**Update (2026-08-13):** P06 directly confirms the same mechanism from a Customer
Specialist/Lead Auditor/TD Assessor segment: the final certification timeline depends heavily
on how quickly the customer responds, and a new MDR (Medical Device Regulation) Article 7
requirement now obliges certification bodies to share a timeline with customers even though
the certification body holds only partial responsibility for the overall duration. Per
[[Definitions]] "Theme threshold," this note is promoted to theme
[[../02_themes/Customers cannot reliably predict the duration of the final certification review step]]
with Confidence Basis Single-interview strong evidence -> Multi-interview (2 of 6 interviews
processed so far). Per [[Definitions]] "Severity/Confidence flag" rule 2 (2+ interviews,
Severity High, Confidence Medium), `validation_status` changes from
`needs-cross-interview-validation` to `needs-validation-before-prioritization`, and the
`validation_question` field is removed in favor of stating the risk directly in the body.
Priority Tier remains P1 (Severity High x Confidence Medium) in `03_pains/_register.md`.

**Theme:** [[../02_themes/Customers cannot reliably predict the duration of the final certification review step]]
**Description:** Unlike earlier service-model phases, which have defined day counts (e.g. 40
working days for the first round, 20 for the second), the final certification-body review step
has no comparably predictable timeline. P02 identifies this as the single biggest pain point
for customers, since customers need to reliably know when an assessment will be finished, when
they will receive a report, and when they will receive a certificate. P06 adds that the final
timeline depends heavily on how quickly the customer responds to requests, so the
certification body holds only partial responsibility for the overall duration, while a new MDR
Article 7 requirement now obliges the certification body to share timeline expectations with
the customer regardless.
**Trigger:** A project reaches the final certification-body review step after earlier
deficiencies have been addressed (P02); a new regulatory requirement to share timelines with
customers surfaces the same unpredictability as a compliance question (P06).
**Impact:** Customers experience follow-up questions and shifting or extended timelines at the
final, most certificate-critical step of the process (P02). Certification staff must now
communicate a timeline to customers under Article 7 while unable to guarantee it, since the
final portion depends on the customer's own response speed (P06).
**Workaround:** None described.

**Severity/Confidence flag:** Severity High with Confidence Medium from two interviews. Per
[[Definitions]] "Severity/Confidence flag" rule 2, this combination requires
`validation_status: needs-validation-before-prioritization`: the mechanism is confirmed twice,
but the specific relationship between customer response speed and the certification body's
compliance obligation under MDR Article 7 (P06) has not yet been cross-checked with additional
interviews.

**Confidence Basis:** Multi-interview — the mechanism (customers cannot reliably predict the
final review step's duration) is now directly confirmed by two distinct interviews (P02, P06)
describing it independently from different angles (customer-facing frustration; regulatory
compliance and shared responsibility).

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 2
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P02, P06

**Representative Quotes:**
> "Ich denk, der größte Pain Point für Kunden ist, wenn die Timeline nicht eingehalten werden, weil der Kunde zuverlässig wissen muss, wann eine Bewertung fertig ist, wann er einen Reporter bekommt, wann er ein Zertifikat bekommt. ... da kommt es oft zu Rückfragen, dann verschiebt sich oder verlängert sich der Slot." - [P02]
>
> Translation: "I think the biggest pain point for customers is when the timeline is not met, because the customer needs to reliably know when an assessment will be finished, when they'll get a report, when they'll get a certificate. ... there are often follow-up questions, and then the slot shifts or extends." - [P02]

> "There is a new Article 7 in the MDR that is requesting us to share a plan with the customers ... to give them the timeline for the certification. But inside these timelines, we have only a partial responsibility. ... this timeline is really long. ... we can solve this issue if we have shared timelines with the customers saying ... you will receive this audit, you will receive this assessment ... we promise you that every round will have three months. ... but then the last part depends on you." - [P06]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- A shared, customer-facing timeline interface showing expected certification milestones,
  which pauses ("stops the clock") while awaiting the customer's response, so that delays
  attributable to the customer are visibly separated from delays attributable to the
  certification body (P06). Explicitly unvalidated.

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Customers frequently fill in standard request forms incorrectly, requiring staff to return them for correction

**Update (2026-08-14):** P08 adds a second confirming interview, from a Client Manager & Lead
Auditor segment, from the form-design side of the same mechanism: the Application Form's
dropdowns do not dynamically filter out logically mutually-exclusive selection combinations,
so data-inconsistent submissions are frequently accepted rather than caught at entry, and
customers are often unclear which application form or information is even required in the
first place. Per [[Definitions]] "Theme threshold," this note is promoted to theme
[[../02_themes/Customers frequently fill in standard request forms incorrectly, requiring staff to return them for correction]]
with Confidence Basis Single-interview strong evidence → Multi-interview (2 of 8 interviews
processed so far; Confidence remains Medium since repetition is below the typical 3+ needed
for High). With 2 interviews and Severity Medium, neither condition in [[Definitions]]
"Severity/Confidence flag" applies, so `validation_status` and `validation_question` are
removed from the frontmatter.

**Theme:** [[../02_themes/Customers frequently fill in standard request forms incorrectly, requiring staff to return them for correction]]
**Description:** Customers submitting a formal service request often fill in the required
form incorrectly, such as marking checkboxes wrong or filling in fields incorrectly. P08
confirms the same mechanism from the form-design side: the Application Form's dropdowns do
not dynamically filter out logically-exclusive combinations, so inconsistent data is often
accepted rather than caught, and customers are frequently unclear which form or information is
required.
**Trigger:** A customer submits a formal service request form as part of the Application
process.
**Impact:** P03 reports having to send the form back for correction fairly often. P08 reports
that data-inconsistent submissions frequently pass through uncaught, and that customer
uncertainty about which form/information is needed adds friction upfront.
**Workaround:** Returning the form to the customer for correction (P03).
**Confidence Basis:** Multi-interview — two distinct interviews (P03, P08) from different
angles (customer-side entry errors; form-design gaps) directly evidence the same mechanism.

**Severity/Confidence flag:** Not applicable. Severity Medium with Confidence Medium does not
meet either condition in [[Definitions]] "Severity/Confidence flag"; no `validation_status` is
set.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 2
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P03, P08

**Representative Quotes:**
> "Ja, also gerade bei den Formblättern, stellen die sich manchmal schlauer und mal dümmer an, da irgendwie die Häkchen richtig zu machen oder das auszufüllen ... das gibt es schon öfter mal dass ich das wieder zurückschicke." - [P03]
>
> Translation: "Yes, especially with the forms, they sometimes manage better and sometimes worse to get the checkboxes right or fill it in correctly ... it happens fairly often that I send it back." - [P03]

> "Das heißt entweder bestimmte Dropdowns, die dann verschwinden, wenn bestimmte Auswahlmöglichkeiten oben das nicht unterstützen, weil wir haben sehr oft die Inkonsistenz von Daten in diesen Formblättern. ... Aber es gibt viele Fälle, die sich einfach logisch ausschließen, die aber nach wie vor oft eingereicht werden können und nicht zu Fehlern kommen." - [P08]
>
> Translation: "So either certain dropdowns disappear when certain selections above don't support them, because we very often have data inconsistency in these forms. ... But there are many cases that are simply logically mutually exclusive, that can nevertheless still often be submitted and are not caught." - [P08]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- A guided intake flow with dynamic follow-up questions that routes the customer to the
  correct form and pre-fills known data, reducing manual form-filling and checkbox errors
  (P03). Explicitly unvalidated.
- Dynamic dropdowns in the Application Form that filter out logically mutually-exclusive
  combinations at entry time, while preserving free-text/comment fields, converging with P03's
  guided-intake idea (P08). Explicitly unvalidated.

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

notes.body:
<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Customers often do not submit all required application documents together

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** Customers can omit a required document from an application submission without
any accompanying explanation, leaving staff unable to tell whether the omission was intentional
(e.g. not applicable) or an oversight, without following up manually.
**Trigger:** A customer submits application documents, and one or more required documents are
missing from the set.
**Impact:** Not directly quantified in this interview; the participant frames the impact
implicitly through a strong preference for a forced-justification safeguard, implying the
current absence of justification for missing documents creates ambiguity or follow-up effort.
**Workaround:** Presumably manual follow-up with the customer to clarify a missing document,
though this is not explicitly described in this interview.
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant expresses a clear,
specific, pre-existing preference for a justification safeguard, indicating this is an observed
recurring gap rather than a hypothetical.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 1
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P08

**Representative Quotes:**
> "Also ich bin großer Fan davon, wenn ich etwas nicht einreiche, dann muss ich zumindest eine Justification dazu schreiben. ... Deswegen, also ich wäre Fan davon, wenn ich kein Dokument hochlade, dann springt ein Justification-Fenster auf und da muss ich auch eintragen." - [P08]
>
> Translation: "I'm a big fan of the idea that if I don't submit something, I at least have to write a justification for it. ... So I'd be in favor of a justification window popping up if I don't upload a document, requiring an entry there too." - [P08]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- A mandatory justification pop-up whenever a required document is not uploaded, so a missing
  document always carries an explicit reason instead of silent absence (P08). Explicitly
  unvalidated.

**Validation question:** Do other staff also find that customers submit application document
sets with items missing, without any indication of whether the omission is intentional,
requiring manual follow-up?

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Customers propose regulatory codes by best guess, requiring correction by certification staff

**Update (2026-08-11):** Confidence Basis Single-interview → Multi-interview; theme link added
(Standalone preliminary finding → confirmed theme); P02 quote and interview ID added;
`validation_status`/`validation_question` removed since the finding is now theme-confirmed and
neither Severity/Confidence flag condition applies (Severity Medium).

**Update (2026-08-12):** P05 adds a third, independent confirmation of the same mechanism
(customers self-assigning EAC codes such as "plastics"/"metals" based on superficial material
match rather than the code's actual manufacturing-technology scope). Per [[Definitions]]
"Sample-relative check," 3 of 5 interviews processed so far (60%) directly and consistently
confirm this mechanism, and repetition is now at the typical 3+ level, so Confidence is raised
from Medium to High. Priority Tier recalculated from P2 to P1 (Severity Medium x Confidence
High) in `03_pains/_register.md`.

**Theme:** [[../02_themes/Customers propose regulatory codes by best guess, requiring correction by certification staff]]
**Description:** Customers assign regulatory codes (e.g. MDA, MDS, MDT) themselves when
submitting a request, but often do not understand the certification body's classification
logic. Codes determine which internally trained assessor is qualified to review a product, so
a customer's incorrect or uninformed code choice creates a deviation that certification staff
must identify and discuss with the customer before assessment planning can proceed correctly.
Regulatory rules also prevent staff from silently overriding a customer's codes "on behalf of"
the customer. A second interview (P02), from a Senior Product Specialist role that inherits
the consequence during assessment, confirms customers frequently cannot judge whether a code
is relevant to their product at all.
**Trigger:** A customer submits self-assigned codes for a product as part of a certification
request.
**Impact:** Certification staff must review and, where necessary, persuade the customer to
correct code assignments before assessor qualification and audit planning can be finalized.
P05 adds that customers routinely over-select codes "vaguely related" to their device (e.g.
picking six codes when realistically only one to three apply), compounding the review burden.
**Workaround:** Staff review submitted codes case by case and negotiate corrections directly
with the customer; an informal internal "Authorization Metrics" document is used to translate
codes to required staff qualifications. P02 additionally reports self-correcting obvious code
errors directly ("ich das quasi auch selber verbessern kann") when other information makes the
correct code unambiguous. P05 notes that certification staff should not assign codes
unilaterally on the customer's behalf, since staff have not seen the product and are not its
experts.
**Confidence Basis:** Not required at Confidence High (Confidence Basis only applies to
Medium). For traceability: 3 of 5 interviews processed so far (P01, P02, P05) directly and
consistently evidence the same mechanism, satisfying both the repetition and sample-relative
checks in [[Definitions]].

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 5
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P01, P02, P05

**Representative Quotes:**
> "Bei den Codes weiß der Kunde immer, was das Richtige ist oder?" / "Natürlich nicht. Kann er nicht oder verbockt er manchmal einfach? Beides." - [P01]
>
> Translation: "With the codes, does the customer always know what's correct?" / "Of course not. Can't he, or does he sometimes just get it wrong? Both." - [P01]

> "Die Zuordnung von Codes in diesem System vom Kunden zu uns kann unterschiedlich sein, weil für uns diese Codes festlegen, welcher Bewerter dafür qualifiziert ist, weil er darauf trainiert wird." - [P01]
>
> Translation: "The assignment of codes in this system from the customer to us can differ, because for us these codes determine which assessor is qualified for it, because that person is trained on it." - [P01]

> "Manchmal ist auch nicht so ganz klar, ist der Code jetzt relevant für das Produkt oder nicht. ... es kann schon zu Fehlern kommen und zurückfragen, und dann ... das kann viel Zeit kosten." - [P02]
>
> Translation: "Sometimes it's also not entirely clear whether a code is relevant for the product or not. ... errors and follow-up questions can occur, and then ... that can cost a lot of time." - [P02]

> "A lot of companies will choose the EAC 14 code for plastics because of this, even because their cartridge is made of plastic. ... those codes are only for the specific manufacturing technologies that they use and most companies don't mold their own plastic cassette housings. They buy those from a supplier. ... They're not actually manufacturing the plastic." - [P05]

> "Realistically, especially for IBD companies, you're probably only going to have like one to three of those applicable [but] companies will pick like 6 because they'll pick like anything that might be vaguely related to their instrument or their device." - [P05]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- An AI-assisted "prescription of codes" or equivalence-based suggestion tool was mentioned as
  potentially valuable. Explicitly unvalidated.
- A dedicated request/contact button to reach the Senior Product Specialist who makes final
  product classification decisions. Explicitly unvalidated.
- Showing customers examples or guidance information at the point of code selection (P02).
  Explicitly unvalidated.
- A first-pass code suggestion derived from the client's entered intended-purpose statement,
  shown as likely/possible tiers, with the client verifying the final selection (P05,
  extending the AI-assisted suggestion idea). Explicitly unvalidated.
- In-context instructions and column/field descriptions shown directly where codes are
  entered, instead of on a separate reference tab (P05). Explicitly unvalidated.

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

notes.body:
<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Customers struggle to correctly format their certification scope statement despite provided instructions

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** Customers must write a certification scope statement following specific
formatting rules (roles, technology, and intended purpose in a required sequence). Even when
staff point out the required format and provide examples, some customers still cannot
correctly apply it to their own product.
**Trigger:** A new client is asked to draft their scope statement as part of Appendix ABC
during onboarding.
**Impact:** Some customers produce an incorrectly formatted scope statement even after
explicit guidance, requiring staff to identify the error and request a correction before the
statement can be used in the certification package. The participant notes results vary widely
by company; some do well, others struggle.
**Workaround:** Staff review the submitted scope statement, point out the specific formatting
rule ("this is what a scope statement is"), and ask the customer to revise it.
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant describes the specific
formatting requirement, the recurring difficulty, and the variability across customers
directly.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 1
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P05

**Representative Quotes:**
> "The two things I see clients struggle with the most with this document are writing their scope statement ... We have very specific rules about how that scope must be formatted ... clients still don't seem to quite be able to pair those things. Even when I specifically pointed out ... this is what a scope statement is ... some companies do pretty well, but some are definitely a struggle." - [P05]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- Showing the required scope-statement structure and a filled-in example directly at the
  point where the customer enters their own scope statement (P05). Explicitly unvalidated.

**Validation question:** Do other onboarding staff also find that customers struggle to write
a correctly formatted scope statement even after being shown the required format and
examples?

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Errors in initial classification surface only late in the assessment

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** When a project is set up with the wrong assessor authorization or the wrong
assessment track at the application stage, the error is often not discovered until the end of
the project. The organization has begun involving the Senior Technical Certifier earlier in
the review to catch this sooner, but the underlying risk of late discovery remains.
**Trigger:** A project is set up with an incorrect assessment track or assessor authorization
at the application stage.
**Impact:** The misclassification surfaces only near project completion, creating rework and
surprises at a stage when correction is more costly.
**Workaround:** The Senior Technical Certifier is now involved earlier in some cases, which
the participant describes as heading in the right direction, but this does not eliminate the
underlying risk.
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant describes the
mechanism directly, including a concrete organizational mitigation already underway.

**Severity/Confidence flag:** Severity High with Confidence Medium from a single interview. Per
[[Definitions]] "Severity/Confidence flag" rule 1, the single-interview gap takes precedence
for `validation_status`, but the severity risk must still be stated here: late-discovered
misclassification can require reworking assessment planning and authorization at a stage where
correction is significantly more costly than at intake.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 2
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P02

**Representative Quotes:**
> "Wenn es am Anfang schon falsch eingespurt wurde, falsche Bewerterautorisierungen oder falsche Schiene quasi vom Assessment, am Ende des Projekts merkt man dann, dass da ist das Risiko quasi, dass man Application falsch eingespurt wurde und später fällt das auf." - [P02]
>
> Translation: "If the track was set incorrectly at the beginning — wrong assessor authorizations or the wrong track for the assessment — you only notice it at the end of the project; there is the risk that the application was set up incorrectly and it only comes to light later." - [P02]

> "Aber da haben wir auch schon verschiedene Sachen in Angriff genommen im späteren Review, das ist der Senior Technical Certifier ... der wird jetzt schon am Anfang mit eingebunden, also das sind Sachen, die auf jeden Fall in die richtige Richtung gehen, ... dass man spätere Überraschungen vermeidet." - [P02]
>
> Translation: "But we've already tackled various things in the later review — the Senior Technical Certifier is now already involved at the beginning, so these are things that are definitely heading in the right direction, ... so that later surprises are avoided." - [P02]

<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: EUDAMED product and certificate data remains incomplete during the platform's transition

**Theme:** [[../02_themes/EUDAMED product and certificate data remains incomplete during the platform's transition]]
**Description:** EUDAMED (European Database on Medical Devices) is not yet a reliable primary
source for customer product and certificate data. P01 reports that customer-entered data is
not fully accurate because of human error and because customers avoid registering products
they intend to discontinue. P02 reports that the platform itself has had major rollout delays
and, until recently, only exposed manufacturer/address data; certificate and product data are
only now becoming available and still need detailed testing. This pain point was split out of
[[Appendix ABC is treated as single source of truth despite being the most error-prone document]],
which originally bundled it with an unrelated Appendix ABC finding.
**Trigger:** Staff consider using EUDAMED as a cross-check or alternative data source for
customer product/certificate information.
**Impact:** Staff cannot yet treat EUDAMED as a dependable cross-check against customer- or
internally-maintained data, limiting its usefulness for reconciliation.
**Workaround:** Staff continue to rely on Appendix ABC and direct customer communication rather
than EUDAMED for product/certificate verification.
**Confidence Basis:** Multi-interview — 2 of 2 interviews processed so far describe EUDAMED
data as currently insufficient, for compatible though distinct reasons (customer data-entry
accuracy vs. platform data-type maturity).

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 2
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P01, P02

**Representative Quotes:**
> "Würdest du sagen, dass deine Kunden ihre Daten in EUDAMED zu 100 Prozent gepflegt haben?" / "Nee. Mindestens dadurch, dass es einen Humanfehler gibt und Leute sich verklicken." - [P01]
>
> Translation: "Would you say your customers maintain their data in EUDAMED 100 percent [accurately]?" / "No. At the very least because there is human error and people misclick." - [P01]

> "Es hat halt große Verzögerung gehabt, das Tool. ... was momentan wirklich bisher nur für Herstellerdaten, Adresse gut war, und die ganzen Sachen mit Zertifikaten, Produktdaten, die kommen jetzt erst zu langsam, müssen wir im Detail testen." - [P02]
>
> Translation: "The tool has had major delays. ... what has really only been good so far for manufacturer data and address, and all the things with certificates and product data are only now slowly coming online; we still need to test them in detail." - [P02]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- Using EUDAMED as a reconciliation/cross-check data source ("Datenabgleich") once its data
  matures, without making it the primary source of truth (P01). Explicitly unvalidated.

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

notes.body:
<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Frequent process and working-instruction changes require re-reading documentation on every project

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** Internal processes and working instructions change often across the many
different project types the participant handles. Even after five and a half years in the
role, the participant reports having to place the current version of the Working Instructions
alongside the work to carry out each project correctly, rather than relying on memorized
procedure.
**Trigger:** A new project of a given type begins, or a working instruction has changed since
the last similar project.
**Impact:** The participant spends recurring time re-reading current instructions on every
project, despite extensive prior experience.
**Workaround:** Keeps the current version of the relevant Working Instructions open alongside
the work.
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant describes this as a
consistent, ongoing personal practice rather than an isolated incident.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 1
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P02

**Representative Quotes:**
> "Ich muss wirklich das so machen, ... ich muss immer wieder die Working Instructions der aktuellen Version auch daneben legen, um die korrekt durchzuführen. ... es kostet schon immer wieder Zeit, ich muss mich immer wieder ein bisschen einlesen." - [P02]
>
> Translation: "I really have to do it that way — I always have to put the current version of the Working Instructions next to me again to carry it out correctly. ... it does cost time again and again, I always have to read up on it a bit again." - [P02]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- An in-tool, guided display of the applicable processes, procedures, working instructions,
  and reports for a given project type (P02). Explicitly unvalidated.

**Validation question:** Do other experienced staff also need to re-read current working
instructions for each new project because processes and instructions change frequently across
project types?

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

notes.body:
<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Independently-edited Appendix ABC copies between auditors and reviewers diverge, causing rejected certification submissions

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** The auditor and the Technical Documentation (TD) reviewer each maintain and
update their own copy of a customer's Appendix ABC over the course of a project. By
submission, the two copies have diverged (different version numbers, different content) and
the certification review team (CRT) receives two conflicting versions for the same company.
This is a distinct mechanism from the separately logged
[[No shared access to the current Appendix ABC version forces staff to rely on colleagues]]
(P02) finding: that finding is about retrieval friction at the start of work (no one-click
access point to the current version), while this finding is about two already-in-progress
copies branching apart and only being reconciled — sometimes unsuccessfully — at submission.
The two are logged as related but are not merged, since they describe different root process
steps.
**Trigger:** The auditor and the TD reviewer each submit their own version of the same
customer's Appendix ABC to the CRT at the end of the review/audit cycle.
**Impact:** The CRT receives two different versions of the same document (e.g. version 6 from
the TD reviewer and version 7 from the auditor) and issues rejects to both parties, who must
then determine collectively which version is correct. This adds rework and delay at the
submission stage of the certification process.
**Workaround:** None described; the divergence is discovered only when the CRT flags the
conflict.
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant describes the
mechanism, a concrete version-number example, and the resulting CRT rejection directly.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 1
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P05

**Representative Quotes:**
> "One of the biggest problems we have sort of post project initiation with the appendix ABC is multiple versions of it out there. ... maybe the one I submit at the end of the audit process ... is different from the one that TD reviewers have. So then I submit version 7 ... TD reviewer did the same. They submit their own, but it's version 6, but they're not the same ... the CRT reviewer has these two appendix ABC's for the same company that are different and then they have to issue rejects to both of us and we all kind of as a collective have to figure out which one's correct." - [P05]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- A single online Appendix ABC that both the auditor and the TD reviewer edit directly,
  removing the need for separate copies to be reconciled at submission (P05, converging with
  the broader Appendix ABC digitization idea already logged under
  [[Appendix ABC is treated as single source of truth despite being the most error-prone document]]).
  Explicitly unvalidated.

**Validation question:** Do other auditor/reviewer pairs also independently maintain their own
copies of a customer's Appendix ABC that diverge by the time of submission, causing the
certification review team to reject conflicting versions?

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

notes.body:
<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Inefficient ad hoc handoff communication between Auditor and Project Coordinator

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** Project Coordinators (PCs), who sit in a different team, need technical input
from the Auditor/Client Manager to set up a project. Because the standard request form does not
capture all the needed technical information, this handoff currently runs through ad hoc email
or Teams calls instead of the form alone.
**Trigger:** A new project needs to be set up and handed to a PC in another team for
administrative processing.
**Impact:** The participant describes the ad hoc email/call handoff as "not particularly
efficient," an intermediate step that would not be necessary if the request form itself
captured all needed information.
**Workaround:** Ad hoc email or Teams calls with the PC to supply missing technical input.
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant describes this as the
current, standard way this handoff works (not a one-off incident), while noting uncertainty
about whether the same holds in all regions.
**Confidence Basis Note:** The participant explicitly flags uncertainty about whether this
practice is regional rather than universal, which is reflected in the validation question
below.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 1
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P08

**Representative Quotes:**
> "Also ich weiß nicht, ob das tatsächlich in allen Regionen bei uns so läuft, aber bei uns ist der Austausch, weil wir die PCs, also die Projektkoordinatorinnen, in einem anderen Team quasi mitnehmen müssen und die brauchen den fachlichen Input, wie sie das Projekt aufsetzen. ... Meiner Ansicht nach, wenn dieses Formblatt die Informationen alle enthält, ist dieser Zwischenschritt nicht mehr notwendig. ... läuft es über E-Mail oder über [Teams] Calls mit den PCs und so weiter, das ist nicht sonderlich effizient." - [P08]
>
> Translation: "I don't know whether that's really how it works in all our regions, but for us the exchange — because we have to bring the PCs, i.e. the Project Coordinators, along from another team, and they need the technical input on how to set up the project. ... In my view, if this form contained all the information, this intermediate step would no longer be necessary. ... it runs over email or [Teams] calls with the PCs and so on, which isn't particularly efficient." - [P08]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- Expanding the standard request form to capture all technical input a Project Coordinator
  needs for project setup, removing the need for a separate ad hoc email/call handoff (P08).
  Explicitly unvalidated.

**Validation question:** Do other Auditors/Client Managers and Project Coordinators also rely
on ad hoc email or Teams calls to hand off technical project-setup input, and would a more
complete standard form reduce that need?

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

notes.body:
<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Internal document templates change without staff or customer guidance on how to complete them

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** Internal document and form templates change periodically, but staff do not
always have time to understand what changed before sending the updated template to customers.
Neither staff nor customers have worked examples for how to fill in some entries. This is
distinct from
[[../03_pains/Frequent process and working-instruction changes require re-reading documentation on every project]]
(P02), which concerns internal working-instruction changes affecting staff's own task
execution, rather than customer-facing template changes and the resulting lack of guidance for
both staff and customers.
**Trigger:** An internal document/form template is updated and then sent to a customer as part
of ongoing certification work.
**Impact:** Staff send customers templates they have not had time to fully review themselves,
without being able to explain unclear entries; customers report feeling unprepared ("fear the
white paper") when facing certain sections for the first time, since no worked example exists.
**Workaround:** None described; the participant reports simply sending the template and
waiting for the customer's answer.
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant raises this directly
and self-critically, including admitting that staff themselves are sometimes not instructed on
how to complete the documents they distribute.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 1
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P06

**Representative Quotes:**
> "It's true that in general there are documents that always change internally in the template. So sometimes if we are in a rush, we don't have time to understand what have been changed in the template. ... we just send them the template and wait for their answer. ... it's not correct to send them a document hoping that they will be able to understand it. ... they don't even have an example on how to fulfill some roles, some entries. And so it's ... sometimes me neither. So the CS is not instructed on how to fulfill those documents." - [P06]

notes.body:
<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: Internal edits to customer data are not tracked or visible to the customer

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** Certification staff sometimes enter or adjust data on the customer's behalf
(e.g. in the internal data collection document), but the current system does not show when a
change was made, what was changed, or by whom, and the customer is not notified when staff
adjust their data.
**Trigger:** A staff member edits a data point (e.g. a code) that was originally submitted by
the customer.
**Impact:** The participant describes this as a "huge problem," since undetected or
unacknowledged changes reduce the system's usefulness over time rather than improving it, and
regulatory responsibility for code correctness formally remains with the certification body in
consultation with the customer, which requires traceability.
**Workaround:** None described beyond informal, ad hoc communication before making a change.
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant volunteers this
unprompted as a significant systemic issue and elaborates on the mechanism.

**Severity/Confidence flag:** Severity High with Confidence Medium from a single interview.
Per [[Definitions]] "Severity/Confidence flag," the single-interview gap takes precedence for
`validation_status`, but the severity risk must still be stated: unacknowledged edits to
regulatory data such as codes carry compliance and trust risk if this generalizes.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 2
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P01

**Representative Quotes:**
> "Ein Riesenproblem in unserem System ist die fehlende Transparenz von Änderungen. Wann wird welche Änderung wie gemacht, wer hat sie gemacht, wie wird sie gehighlightet, der Kunde sieht nicht, wenn wir was anpassen." - [P01]
>
> Translation: "A huge problem in our system is the lack of transparency of changes. When is which change made and how, who made it, how is it highlighted, the customer doesn't see when we adjust something." - [P01]

> "Also im Endeffekt müsste man dann eine nicht Service Request, aber eine Specification Request über sowas stellen können. Also irgendwas, bei dem der Typ sagen kann, hey, die following Concerns, die following Request habe ich, lieber Kunde, gib mir entweder 'ne Response oder buch dir 'n Meeting." - [P01]
>
> Translation: "So in the end one would need to be able to raise not a service request, but a specification request for something like this. Something where the person can say, hey, here are the following concerns, the following request I have, dear customer, either give me a response or book a meeting." - [P01]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
- A read-receipt-style acknowledgment notification to the customer when staff change a data
  point, with a case-by-case decision on whether the customer must be informed. Explicitly
  unvalidated.
- A "Specification Request" workflow letting staff formally raise a concern/change request that
  the customer must respond to or schedule a meeting for. Explicitly unvalidated.

**Validation question:** Do other internal staff or customers confirm the lack of
visibility/notification when internal staff edit customer-provided data?

## Reference
See [[Definitions]] for severity and confidence criteria.

frontmatter.validation_question: Do other staff working on international projects also experience multi-week to multi-month delays from cross-organizational handoffs and inconsistent regional response times?

notes.body:
<!-- Describe observations in plain, third-person language. Keep validation and inference separate. -->

# Pain Point: International projects lose weeks or months to cross-organizational handoffs and inconsistent regional responsiveness

**Theme:** `Standalone preliminary finding`
**Description:** International projects involve many organizational interfaces (e.g.
subcontractors, local project handlers, regional teams) that are not well interlocked with
each other. In one project, a required subcontract was repeatedly requested but took about
three months to arrive, blocking work that should have been able to start within half a day.
Separately, response times vary significantly by region; the participant describes
consistently slow responses when working with some regions, sometimes waiting weeks to months
for a result because requests must first pass through a manager.
**Trigger:** A project requires coordination across organizational or regional boundaries
(e.g. subcontracting work, or requesting input from a regional team).
**Impact:** Work is blocked or delayed for weeks to months, well beyond what the participant
considers a reasonable turnaround (e.g. half a day for a subcontract).
**Workaround:** Repeated follow-up requests; no structural fix described.
**Confidence Basis:** Single-interview strong evidence — the participant provides one detailed
case example (subcontract delay) plus a general pattern description (regional response time),
both pointing to the same underlying mechanism of too many poorly-interlocked interfaces in
international projects.

**Severity/Confidence flag:** Severity High with Confidence Medium from a single interview. Per
[[Definitions]] "Severity/Confidence flag" rule 1, the single-interview gap takes precedence
for `validation_status`, but the severity risk must still be stated here: a three-month delay
on a blocking dependency is a significant, project-level impact if this pattern generalizes
across international projects.

## Evidence
**Quotes Logged:** 3
<!-- Citation count for traceability, not corroboration. Many quotes from one interview_id is NOT multiple confirmations; see Definitions.md "Quote Count vs. Interview Count". -->
**Interview IDs:** P02

**Representative Quotes:**
> "Ich hatte ein Projekt, da haben wir wiederholt immer wieder nachgefragt und wir haben kein Subcontract bekommen. Ohne den können wir eigentlich, ... können wir auch nicht arbeiten. ... Ich denk, da hat 3 Monate gebraucht, bis dann Subcontract da war, was eigentlich noch, keine Ahnung, an dem halben Tag gehen sollte oder könnte." - [P02]
>
> Translation: "I had a project where we repeatedly asked and never received a subcontract. Without it we basically ... cannot work either. ... I think it took 3 months until the subcontract was there, which should actually be able to happen within half a day." - [P02]

> "Da sind sehr viele Schnittstellen, wo die Prozesse nicht gut miteinander verhakt sind oder das Interface nicht so gut funktioniert, denke ich, dass so das der größte Punkt fast." - [P02]
>
> Translation: "There are very many interfaces where the processes are not well interlocked with each other, or the interface doesn't work so well — I think that's almost the biggest issue." - [P02]

> "Schwieriger wird es dann, wenn es in die Regionen geht ... wenn es Richtung Indien geht, habe ich jetzt persönlich eher schlechte Erfahrungen gemacht, [ich] warte mal so lang auf die Antwort und dann geht es wieder erst zum Manager. ... da wartet man wirklich Wochen und Monate, bis man ein Ergebnis oder einen Output hat." - [P02]
>
> Translation: "It gets more difficult when it goes to [other] regions ... when it's toward India, I've personally had rather bad experiences — you wait a long time for a response and then it first goes to the manager again. ... you really wait weeks and months until you get a result or an output." - [P02]

## Candidate Solution Ideas (unvalidated)
<!-- Optional, non-binding ideas only. These are NOT recommendations. A validated recommendation lives inside its anchor insight, never here. -->
[None currently logged.]

**Validation question:** Do other staff working on international projects also experience
multi-week to multi-month delays from cross-organizational handoffs and inconsistent regional
response times?
